new_statements.quote: Two verb types were distinguished for Ambai on the basis of underlying stress which account for the morphophonemic variations which occur with the infixes /-u-/ and /-i-/ in 5.1.3.1.2. A comparison of verbs in Ambai with cognate forms in the other Yapen languages indicates that the two stress patterns are also present in the other languages. All Yapen languages, except Busami, exhibit different patterns of interaction between the infixes /-u-/ and /-i-/ with verbs with the initial syllable of the stem stressed and those with the initial syllable of the verb unstressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No default stress position is stated for Munggui. Silzer claims, from 1981 survey notes, that Munggui (listed as 'Mun.' in Figure A.2 alongside Woi, Pom, Papuma, Busami, Ansus, Wandamen, Serui-Laut, Ambai) shares the Ambai split of verb stems into a class with the stem-initial syllable stressed and a class with it unstressed, the class being diagnosed by whether the stem vowel survives or assimilates when the 2sg/3sg infixes -u-/-i- are inserted; i.e. stress on verb stems is lexically specified. For Munggui the figure shows only the 'stressed' paradigm (e-tanang / t-u-anang / t-y-anang 'to plant') and the 1sg of the 'unstressed' verb (e-matai 'to fear'), so the contrast is asserted for Munggui by generalisation, not demonstrated.
new_statements.exceptions: Busami is excepted from the Yapen-wide claim; nothing else.
new_statements.domain_note: Verb stems (underlying stress as a lexical property of the stem), inferred from infix morphophonemics; nothing on nouns, on surface word stress, or on citation forms. Data are 1981 survey notes (Ajamiseba & Silzer), not a description of Munggui.
new_statements.identity_note: Munggui proper (mung1269); Anceaux 1961: 7 and Voorhoeve 1975: 57-58 distinguish two dialects (Windesi + Murui/Musui vs Munggui + Puramati). Silzer 1983 does not say which village his 1981 'Mun.' data came from. Glottolog alt. name Natabui is a village Anceaux assigns to a Marau dialect, not to Munggui.

sources.citation: Kamholz, David. 2014. Austronesians in Papua: diversification and change in South Halmahera-West New Guinea. PhD dissertation, UC Berkeley.
sources.note: Munggui data second-hand (Silzer 1983; Anceaux 1961a; ACD). Sec. 5.4 pp. 117-118 lists SHWNG languages with described penultimate stress (Buli, Sawai, Taba, Ambai, Wandamen, Waropen, Warembori) -- Munggui not among them; p. 38 reports Price & Donohue 2008 that 'other languages of Yapen also have complex stress systems'; pp. 138-139 place Munggui in Proto-Central Yapen. Nothing Munggui-specific on stress.

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Languages of Irian Jaya: checklist, preliminary classification, language maps, wordlists. Pacific Linguistics B-31. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Checklist entry 179 MUNGGUI (pp. 57-58): two dialects (Windesi, Musui / Munggui, Puramati), 650+ speakers, source Anceaux 1961. Comparative wordlists have no Munggui column. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Anceaux, J. C. 1961. The linguistic situation in the islands of Yapen, Kurudu, Nau and Miosnum, New Guinea. Verhandelingen KITLV 35. 's-Gravenhage: Nijhoff.
sources.note: Munggui data were 'Two 100 Lists, one filled in by a mantri of the anti-malaria service, the other by the village schoolmaster' (p. 3); p. 7 names the language, villages and two dialects (Windesi+Murui vs Munggui+Puramati), 650+ speakers; p. 14: 'Stress-accent, vowel pitch and vowel length... are not indicated' in the wordlist. The lexical-accent remark on p. 7 is about Papuma only. Nothing on Munggui stress.
